## Seite 26

  • OpenHands: SSE via LiteLLM wrapper, now with first-class streaming (an LLM.stream
    field and token deltas forwarded through on_token callbacks) plus an OpenAI Responses
    path. Supports prompt caching markers for Anthropic models.
  • Hermes: five owned transport implementations; a ∼23-value FailoverReason enum drives
    classified recovery (compress vs. rotate credential vs. fallback chain vs. abort).
  • Pi: nine wire-protocol implementations with a partial-json salvage parser for streamed
    tool arguments—paired with the truncation guard of Section 6, since salvaged arguments can
    validate while incomplete.
  • OpenCode: Vercel AI SDK streamText owns dispatch; token-granular part deltas are per-
    sisted and re-served over SSE by the embedded server, so every client (TUI, web, IDE) replays
    the same stream.
  • OpenClaw: ACP delta events for text, thought, and tool calls; provider-specific transport
    streams handle the underlying SSE/WebSocket layer.

7.5   Advanced API Features
The single-provider systems exploit features unavailable to multi-provider abstractions:
    Claude Code’s extended-thinking integration exposes a budget_tokens parameter that con-
trols how much internal reasoning the model performs before responding; while LiteLLM does pass
through Anthropic’s thinking block, surfacing budget_tokens as a first-class scaffold knob still
requires Anthropic-specific conditional code in any multi-provider design. Codex’s reasoning-effort
enum spans minimal/low/medium/high/xhigh, extended in mid-2026 with max and ultra—and
ultra is not just more reasoning: the model catalog describes it as maximum reasoning with auto-
matic sub-agent task delegation, an effort level that changes orchestration behavior, unique in the cor-
pus. Mistral Vibe’s per-model thinking field now spans five levels (off/low/medium/high/max)
mapped onto Mistral’s reasoning_effort enum, and Pi normalizes the whole landscape behind
a unified seven-level scale translated through ten per-API thinkingFormat dialects. Codex im-
plements prompt caching via a prompt_cache_key derived from the session’s ThreadId (with an
explicit override hook for delegate and guardian sessions); this is a lighter-weight strategy than
Claude Code’s Blake2b-hashed static/dynamic boundary. Aider’s vision support warrants a
note: when the active model’s supports_vision attribute is set (via LiteLLM metadata), Aider
accepts image files in the chat, handles MIME types, and passes them to the model. The support
is model-gated rather than unconditional, hence marked “Opt.” in Table 17; Mistral Vibe joined
the vision column in v2.14–2.18 (TUI @-mentions, clipboard paste, ACP inline image blocks), and
Mini-SWE-Agent retains an opt-in, default-off multimodal path (a multimodal_regex expanding
tagged content into image blocks), so no corpus system is unconditionally text-only. Gemini CLI
exposes extended thinking (with thought-part stripping to keep caches clean) and then routes the
choice of model itself through ModelRouterService; that treatment of per-request model selection
as classifier-driven runtime scheduling remains unique in the corpus (OpenHands’s RouterLLM
profiles route by configuration, not per-query classification), now extending to a managed on-device
runtime (a gemini gemma command group provisions a local LiteRT-LM server, and the routing
chain can use the local Gemma model as its query classifier). On the observability side, Gemini CLI
emits OpenTelemetry traces alongside per-token cost accounting. Mistral Vibe also instruments
its agent loop, tool execution, and hooks with OpenTelemetry (agent_span/tool_span/hook_span
async context managers with an OTLP exporter and GenAI semantic-convention attributes), and
Pi contributes the corpus’s most unusual observability metric: a per-turn cache-miss dollar-waste
audit that prices every avoidable cache invalidation.

8     Tool and Action Systems
The tool system defines what the agent can actually do: which actions it can invoke and how they
are executed. This subsystem absorbs a large share of the engineering effort in every mature agent
we studied.

8.1     Tool Count Spectrum
Figure 3 illustrates the spectrum from minimalist to maximal tool designs. The systems span from
a single bash tool to 109+ tools including media processing and channel integrations—with Pi
making the sparse end a philosophy (seven tools built, four exposed by default, everything else an
extension) and Hermes pushing the general-purpose end to 69 built-ins behind a toolset layer that
scopes what each platform’s model actually sees.

                       Pi                Aider                         Codex             Claude Code
      Mini-SWE-Agent Mistral Vibe               OpenCode

                1       7         12       13         17        25         27       35         43          69             109

Figure 3: Tool count spectrum (July 2026). Numbers indicate distinct built-in tools or edit formats;

8.2     Tool Interface Architectures
Tool interfaces range from almost no abstraction—Mini-SWE-Agent sends everything through
a single shell call (subprocess.Popen(shell=True), wrapped only to kill the process group on
timeout)—to rich typed contracts. Claude Code’s 43 tools each declare validation, permission
checking, concurrency safety, and UI rendering as separate interface concerns. Codex uses Rust
trait objects for runtime polymorphism—the registry stores Arc<dyn CoreToolRuntime> where
CoreToolRuntime: ToolExecutor, the abstraction now extracted into a standalone codex-tools
crate shared with code mode and extensions. Gemini CLI routes calls through a state-machine
Scheduler that walks each invocation through deterministic Validating → Executing → Complet-
ed/Errored phases. Mistral Vibe adds tree-sitter-parsed bash—an asyncio.create_subprocess_shell-
based execution path that uses tree_sitter_bash to validate command structure before spawning—
and fine-grained permission scopes (command pattern, file pattern, URL allowlist, directory con-
tainment). Hermes’s singleton registry separates registration from exposure: 69 tools self-register
at import, a toolset layer scopes what each platform’s model sees, per-tool availability probes
(30-second TTL with a last-good grace window) keep one flaky docker version from stripping a
toolset, and a coercion layer repairs schema drift ("42"→42) motivated by observed open-model
output. Pi gives each of its seven tools a pluggable Operations interface (BashOperations,
EditOperations, . . . )—the single remoting seam through which SSH, container, and micro-VM
extensions relocate execution without touching the tools. OpenCode registers 17 first-party tools
with Effect schemas and swaps the tool surface per model: GPT-family models receive a port of
Codex’s apply_patch DSL and lose edit/write entirely (Section 8.4). The spectrum reflects the
simplicity-versus-capability axis: more interface surface means more safety guarantees but more
engineering cost.

8.3     Deferred Tool Loading
Claude Code introduced deferred tool loading: tools marked with shouldDefer = true are ex-
cluded from the initial system prompt. The LLM discovers them on-demand via ToolSearchTool,

which supports keyword search and direct selection (select:<tool_name>). This reduces prompt
size significantly: of 43 tools, only a core subset is loaded initially. The deferred tool set is cached
via getDeferredToolsCacheKey(), invalidated when the set changes.
    The April edition presented this as a Claude Code exclusive; by July it is a spreading pat-
tern with independent implementations. Codex marks tools (by default, MCP tools) with a
defer_loading flag and exposes a tool_search tool backed by a BM25 lexical index over tool
specs—the same prompt economics with ranked search instead of substring matching. Hermes
generalizes the idea with a threshold: when MCP and plugin schemas would exceed 10% of the
context window, they collapse into three bridge tools (tool_search/tool_describe/tool_call)
searched by an inlined BM25 engine. OpenCode defers skills (catalog lists name and description
only; a native skill tool fetches bodies) and treats its experimental code mode as MCP-catalog
deferral: instead of exposing every MCP tool, one execute tool runs model-written scripts against
the catalog. Mistral Vibe’s defer_mcp flag, by contrast, defers only MCP connection at startup
for latency, not prompt visibility—once integrated, every MCP tool is model-visible, so we no longer
group it with the prompt-level deferral pattern.

## Seite 29

The editing landscape reorganized between snapshots. The April edition described Mis-
tral Vibe and Gemini CLI as a “polymorphic-by-degree” pair—coarse whole-file tool plus fuzzy
fine-grained patch tool. Neither half survived the quarter. Mistral Vibe deleted its SEARCH/RE-
PLACE tool outright and converged on Claude Code’s exact unique-substring contract (with a
replace_all escape hatch and a now create-only write_file): a rare observable case of a produc-
tion harness migrating between editing-strategy clusters, and evidence that stronger models shift
the optimum from tool-side drift tolerance toward strict contracts.6 Gemini CLI’s edit, on closer
inspection, is an old/new-string tool with a cascading matcher (exact → whitespace-flexible → regex
→ fuzzy) that ends in something no other system had: an LLM edit-fixer subcall that repairs the
failed old/new pair against a model-supplied instruction—the corpus’s first in-tool LLM-assisted
edit repair.

The fuzzy-cascade family and its visible lineage. Where Mistral Vibe left, two new-
comers arrived with the corpus’s most elaborate drift tolerance, and their source code documents
its ancestry. OpenCode’s nine-stage replacer cascade (exact → line-trimmed → block-anchor
→ whitespace/indentation/escape-normalized → context-aware, under Levenshtein 0.65 with a
disproportionate-match guard) carries header comments crediting Cline and Gemini CLI evals;
Hermes’s nine-strategy chain is annotated “inspired by OpenCode.” Editing machinery now has
a visible cross-harness genealogy—convergence by inheritance, not just rediscovery. Pi stakes out
a third position: no similarity threshold at all, only Unicode/whitespace canonicalization (NFKC,
smart quotes, trailing whitespace), with replacements computed in normalized space overlaid line-
wise onto the original bytes so untouched lines keep their exact original whitespace—plus an async
diff preview rendered before the tool executes.
    Aider’s RelativeIndenter still deserves special attention. It converts absolute indentation to
relative changes using Unicode markers (default: left arrow ←, selected to avoid collisions with file
content). The make_relative() method tracks indent differences between consecutive lines, and
make_absolute() reconstructs original indentation. This enables edit blocks to work across different
indentation levels, a common failure mode for other systems. Combined with fuzzy matching via
diff_match_patch (threshold 0.95, distance 500), this creates a robust editing pipeline.
Observation 4. The file-editing strategy is one of the most important determinants of code-
modification accuracy in an SWE agent, and model-aware polymorphism is no longer Aider’s
alone. Aider selects the edit format per model through a prompt-class factory; OpenCode
reaches the same insight through the tool registry, swapping the toolset per model (GPT-family
models get a Codex-style patch DSL and lose the string-replacement tools entirely). The cor-
pus’s editing machinery now shows explicit cross-harness lineage (Hermes’s matcher “inspired
by OpenCode”; OpenCode’s cascade crediting Cline and Gemini CLI), and it is in visible
motion: Mistral Vibe migrated from fuzzy SEARCH/REPLACE to Claude Code-style ex-
act matching within one quarter, while Gemini CLI added LLM-assisted edit repair. Aider’s
RelativeIndenter remains the most sophisticated solution to indentation-sensitive matching.

## Seite 31

it drives Seatbelt profiles through /usr/bin/sandbox-exec. On Windows it uses restricted-token
processes. Protected paths (.git, .agents, .codex) are re-marked read-only even when they sit
inside a writable root. The result is OS-level isolation without the overhead of a container runtime.

Gemini CLI joins Codex as the second cross-platform sandboxer. Gemini CLI’s
SandboxManager implements the same three-platform stack as Codex: Docker or Bubblewrap on
Linux, Seatbelt via /usr/bin/sandbox-exec on macOS, restricted-token processes on Windows.
Where Codex bakes its policy into Starlark execpolicy rules (Section 10), Gemini CLI layers a
TOML-based per-mode sandbox policy (plan / default / accepting_edits) plus environment
scrubbing of provider credentials (name-pattern regexes over TOKEN/SECRET/KEY/AUTH/CREDENTIAL,
a denylist, and GitHub-token value regexes) before each command runs. Gemini CLI’s sandbox
investment is meaningfully lighter than Codex’s because Gemini CLI reuses Node’s child-process
API and OS-provided binaries rather than implementing low-level namespace plumbing itself;
Codex pays for its larger footprint in vendored-Bubblewrap integration and Rust-native names-
pace control. The April edition observed that the two largest systems in the corpus were also
the two with native cross-platform sandboxing and asked whether the correlation was structural;
the expanded corpus answers no: Hermes (∼642K lines) ships zero OS-level isolation primitives,
delegating containment to six pluggable execution backends while investing its safety budget in
content-borne threats, and OpenCode (∼578K lines) is policy-only. Size predicts some large safety
investment, not specifically a sandbox; Section 10 maps where each system spends instead.

9     Memory and Context Management
Every agent we looked at runs into the same problem eventually: the conversation outgrows the
context window. The literature offers two broad families of solutions: tiered memory architectures
(such as MemGPT [74], which shuffles data between an in-context working set and an external
store) and prompt-compression methods (such as LLMLingua [75], which shortens text before it
reaches the model). The eleven systems in the corpus implement four practical strategies (Figure 4),
which we present in roughly increasing order of sophistication.

9.1   Strategy Taxonomy

             Linear           Summarization             Condensation             Compaction
            No pruning         Recursive halving        10 → 3 condensers        Threshold-based

         Mini-SWE-Agent        Aider, OpenClaw            OpenHands           Claude Code, Codex,
                                                                            Gemini CLI, Mistral Vibe,
                                                                             Hermes, Pi, OpenCode

               Simple                                                              Sophisticated

Figure 4: Memory management strategies ordered by sophistication. Seven of the eleven systems—
the four provider-native harnesses and all three systems added in this revision—converge on
threshold-triggered LLM compaction: a de facto standard for production-grade context manage-
ment, though each newcomer hybridizes it with traits of the other strategies (iterative summary
merging, pluggable engines, session-tree substrates).

9.2   Linear History (Mini-SWE-Agent)
Mini-SWE-Agent makes no attempt to manage context. The full message list grows unboundedly,
relying on the LLM’s native context window (up to 1M tokens with the Claude 4 family). This
simplicity enables perfect reproducibility and straightforward trajectory analysis, a deliberate choice
for a research baseline system.

## Seite 32

9.3   Recursive Summarization (Aider)
Aider’s ChatSummary class implements a recursive halving algorithm. When the message history
exceeds max_tokens (default: 1024), it splits messages into two halves by token count, keeping the
tail (most recent 50%) intact. The head is summarized via an LLM call (summarize_all()). If the
combined summary + tail still exceeds the limit, the process recurses up to 3 levels. A separate
“weak model” (e.g., GPT-3.5-turbo) can be configured for cost-efficient summarization.

9.4   Pluggable Condensation (OpenHands)
OpenHands pioneered pluggable memory management through an abstract Condenser base class.
The V0 application shipped ten implementations; the V1 SDK consolidated the zoo to three
(NoOpCondenser, LLMSummarizingCondenser, PipelineCondenser) over a RollingCondenser
base—a telling simplification, most of the specialized variants having proven unnecessary. Two up-
grades came with the consolidation: condensation is itself event-sourced (CondensationRequest/Condensation
events in the log, so compression history is replayable), and the condenser doubles as error recov-
ery—context-window overflows and malformed-history errors trigger a condensation rather than a
crash. The summarizing condenser also gained a token-count trigger (max_tokens) alongside its
event-count threshold, aligning OpenHands with the threshold-compaction family below.

9.5   Threshold Compaction (Seven Systems)
Claude Code’s compaction triggers when the running token estimate enters a buffer below the
model’s effective context window (AUTOCOMPACT_BUFFER_TOKENS = 13 000, with an env-overridable
percent threshold for testing). The process: (1) strip images from messages (replace with [image]
markers), (2) group messages by API round, (3) invoke the LLM to generate a conversation sum-
mary, (4) create a SystemCompactBoundaryMessage separating pre-compaction history from the
summary. Post-compaction cleanup restores up to 5 files (POST_COMPACT_TOKEN_BUDGET = 50 000)
and truncates skills to a per-skill 25 000-token budget.
   Codex supports both local in-process and cloud-based summarization via a dedicated
/responses/compact endpoint, with model_auto_compact_token_limit controlling when sum-
marization triggers (the separate /memories/trace_summarize endpoint serves the memories
pipeline of Section 9.6); a remote-compaction v2 path and per-thread rollout token budgets (with
remaining-budget reminders and turn aborts on exhaustion) were added in the spring 2026 releases.

Gemini CLI: Multi-Stage Context Pipeline. Gemini CLI’s context management is more so-
phisticated than simple compression. At the top level, a ChatCompressionService fires when his-
tory exceeds 50% of the model’s token limit, calls Gemini to generate a state snapshot, and preserves
the most recent 30% of history verbatim (a token-budget truncation pre-pass and a PreCompress
hook now fire before compression). Beneath this, a dedicated context-processors module implements
a multi-stage context distillation pipeline with pluggable processors (rolling summary, node distilla-
tion, node truncation, blob degradation, tool masking, state snapshot), consolidated in v0.43–0.45
into a ContextManager that maintains a pristine-versus-active context graph in a working buffer,
runs processors through an orchestrator with hysteresis-based trigger damping, and replaces static
chars-per-token estimates with an adaptive token calculator calibrated against observed API to-
ken counts. A separate ContextCompressionService tracks per-file compression levels (FULL,
PARTIAL, SUMMARY, EXCLUDED), providing finer granularity than Claude Code’s binary
compacted/uncompacted split, and a pluggable AgentHistoryProvider interface lets extensions
substitute their own compression logic.

Mistral Vibe: Middleware-Triggered, Now Two-Tier and Reactive. Mistral Vibe’s
AutoCompactMiddleware checks context_tokens >= auto_compact_threshold before each turn;
the compaction routine itself, extracted into a CompactionManager, has grown three refinements
since April: the post-compaction state is a context envelope that re-injects prior user messages

                                                 32

---

## Seite 33

alongside the summary (so original task goals survive resets), a cache-friendly primary summariza-
tion falls back to a dedicated tool-less summarizer, and the same routine fires reactively when a
turn overflows the context window mid-flight. The integration through the middleware pipeline
remains architecturally cleaner than in-loop checks: compaction is just another turn policy. Mis-
tral Vibe’s complementary RewindManager creates filesystem-level checkpoints per user message
and supports rewinding with optional file restoration—now forkable to a new session and exposed
over ACP so IDE clients can drive the rewind. Once unique, checkpointing now has a finer-grained
sibling: OpenCode maintains a shadow git repository per project (separate –git-dir over the real
worktree) snapshotting at pre-stream, step start, and step finish, yielding per-step patch parts and
full conversation-plus-filesystem revert.

Hermes: Lineage Compaction. Hermes lands in the threshold family (trigger at 50% of con-
text minus max-tokens, 64K floor; protect the first three messages plus a token-budgeted tail;
iterative auxiliary-model summary capped at min(5% of context, 12K tokens)) but adds a con-
struct no other system has: compaction does not rewrite the transcript—it ends the session. Each
compaction closes the current SQLite session (end_reason=’compression’) and rotates to a child
chained by parent_session_id; lineage helpers walk the ancestry, and session search deduplicates
across it. Context management and session persistence become one mechanism, and no history
is ever destroyed. The engine is pluggable (a ContextEngine ABC), echoing OpenHands’s con-
densers.

Pi: Compaction over a Session Tree. Pi triggers at contextWindow − 16,384 tokens (keeping
20K recent), with two traits borrowed from the other strategies: summaries are iteratively merged—
the update prompt re-ingests the previous summary rather than re-summarizing from scratch (a
recursive-summarization trait)—and a session_before_compact hook lets extensions veto or re-
place the result entirely (a pluggable-condensation trait). The distinctive substrate is the session
itself: an append-only JSONL tree where every entry carries id/parentId and a movable leaf pointer
defines the active branch. /tree navigation, /fork, and /clone unify what other harnesses imple-
ment as three separate features (checkpointing, rewind, alternative exploration), and abandoning
a branch optionally generates an LLM branch summary spliced into the new position, so explo-
ration is never lost—with the explicit trade-off that filesystem state is not restored. Cumulative
<read-files>/<modified-files> lists persist as structured memory across compactions.

OpenCode: Anchored Incremental Summaries. OpenCode triggers at limit.input minus
a reserved-output margin, using a chars/4 estimate (no tokenizer exists anywhere in the tree), and
produces the corpus’s most explicitly incremental summary: the previous summary is passed back
in a <previous-summary> block and merged (“preserve still-true details, remove stale details”)
by a hidden, all-tools-denied compaction agent, into mandated Markdown sections (Objective /
Important Details / Work State / Next Move / Relevant Files). A verbatim tail of two user turns is
preserved; opt-in pruning soft-deletes old tool outputs, protecting the newest 40K tokens and firing
only if more than 20K are reclaimable.

9.6   Persistent Memory Pipelines
The April edition of this study could describe cross-session memory in one sentence per system:
a Markdown context file here, a transcript store there. Three months later, persistent memory
is where the provider-native systems are differentiating most aggressively, and the designs diverge
instructively on a single axis: who writes the memory, and who reviews it.
    Codex runs the most autonomous design. A background two-phase pipeline extracts structured
memories from recent session rollouts (per-rollout LLM extraction into a SQLite state database,
with leased jobs, retry backoff, and secret redaction) and then consolidates them into filesystem arti-
facts under a git-baselined ~/.codex/memories/ root—the consolidation performed by a sandboxed
internal sub-agent (no approvals, no network, local-write-only) reviewing a git-style workspace diff.

                                                  33

---

## Seite 34

Memories are injected into new sessions with citation tracking and usage-based ranking. Codex is
thus the first system in the corpus whose long-term memory is maintained by an agent rather than
by code; an experimental “chronicle” sidecar extends the same machinery toward passive screen
context.
     Gemini CLI moved in the opposite governance direction. Its April-era callable save_memory
tool is gone—the system prompt now states flatly that no such tool exists—replaced by (a) the model
editing GEMINI.md or a private per-project MEMORY.md index directly with ordinary edit tools, and
(b) an asynchronous skill-extraction sub-agent that mines completed session transcripts and emits
canonical patch files into a per-project .inbox/, which the user reviews and applies via /memory.
Where Codex lets an agent consolidate memory autonomously, Gemini CLI inserts a human-gated
review inbox between extraction and persistence—the only such design in the corpus.
     Hermes keeps persistent memory deliberately tiny and cache-friendly: two bounded Markdown
files (MEMORY.md, 2,200 characters; USER.md, 1,375) injected as a frozen snapshot, so mid-session
writes hit disk without invalidating the prompt cache. Conversation recall is deterministic—a
session_search tool over trigger-maintained SQLite FTS5 tables (BM25, plus trigram indexing for
CJK), “no LLM calls anywhere”—and embeddings exist only in opt-in memory plugins. OpenClaw
ships an Active Memory plugin (present, we note for the record, since the very April release our
earlier edition audited) that runs a dedicated memory sub-agent immediately before the main reply,
plus its older opt-in LanceDB conversation-memory extension. OpenHands folds memory into its
context-file convention: a <MEMORY> prompt section instructs the model to persist durable facts into
AGENTS.md itself. Claude Code persists per-project memory directories of Markdown facts; Pi
and Mini-SWE-Agent deliberately persist nothing beyond the session substrate.
Observation 5. Persistent memory has replaced compaction as the frontier of context engineer-
ing. Compaction designs have converged (seven of eleven systems use threshold-triggered LLM
summarization, increasingly with incremental merging); what now differentiates the field is the
memory write path. Four governance models coexist: agent-maintained (Codex: a sandboxed
sub-agent consolidates memories over a git-baselined store), human-gated (Gemini CLI: extrac-
tion sub-agent writes to a patch inbox the user reviews via /memory), model-direct-but-bounded
(Hermes: character-capped Markdown snapshots, frozen per session for cache hygiene; Open-
Hands, Claude Code: context-file conventions), and pre-turn agentic recall (OpenClaw’s
Active Memory sub-agent). Notably, none of the eleven uses embedding-based retrieval as its
primary memory substrate—the deterministic-retrieval finding of Observation 9 extends from
code to memory, with SQLite full-text search (Hermes) as the production ceiling.

9.7   Repository Context
Beyond conversation history, agents must manage code context:

  • Aider RepoMap: Tree-sitter-based symbol indexing with diskcache (SQLite v4)—still the
    only ranked repository map in the corpus. Symbols are ranked by relevance to the current
    conversation. Token budget is adaptive (map_tokens, default 1024) with a map_mul_no_files
    multiplier for large repositories.
  • Claude Code Memory System: Auto-discovers CLAUDE.md files via a dedicated claudemd
    subsystem (managed, user, and project scopes traversed from the working directory), injected
    as nested memory attachments with deduplication; the separate memdir machinery manages
    the per-project persistent auto-memory directory.
  • Codex Instructions: Hierarchical AGENTS.md instructions—precisely, a concatenation from
    the project root down to the working directory (nested content appended last, so “precedence”
    holds only by position), plus an AGENTS.override.md escape hatch and configurable root
    markers and fallback filenames.
  • Gemini CLI Context Files: Three-scope GEMINI.md merge (global, extension, project)

       gated by folder trust, plus JIT injection of subdirectory context files through tool output and
       the private MEMORY.md project index.
   • Mistral Vibe JIT Discovery: Top-level AGENTS.md in the prompt (user and project scopes),
     and—since v2.19—nested AGENTS.md files surfaced just-in-time when read_file touches files
     beneath them.
   • Hermes Hierarchy with Threat Scanning: First-found-wins walk (.hermes.md/HERMES.md
     to the git root, then AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules); every context file is scanned
     for prompt-injection patterns and blocked wholesale on a match; a subdirectory hint tracker

     tags; loading of repo-controlled configuration (extensions, skills) is trust-gated, but context

   • OpenCode Pull-Based Attach: AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md/CONTEXT.md walk-up (first file-

   • OpenHands Third-Party Ingestion: the skills subsystem ingests AGENTS.md, .cursorrules,

   • OpenClaw Transcripts:     JSONL transcript files persisted per agent/session at
     ~/.openclaw/agents/<agentId>/sessions/<sessionKey>.jsonl.

10      Safety and Permission Models
Safety mechanisms become important in direct proportion to the autonomy the agent is given. A
recent line of academic work has formalized the threat model: indirect prompt injection through
file or web content [77], AgentDojo [76] as a dynamic evaluation environment for injection attacks
and defenses, risk-awareness benchmarks like R-Judge [78], and ToolSword’s [79] catalog of tool-
use safety failure modes. The corpus covers a wide range, from systems with essentially no safety
controls to multi-layered architectures.

10.1     Claude Code: Three-Layered Permission System
Claude Code implements the most architecturally elegant safety system, with three layers (Fig-
ure 5):

 Fastest, least context     Layer 1: Static Hook Rules (PreToolUse pattern matching)

                           Layer 2: LLM-based Permission Classifier (allow / ask / deny)   Claude Code

Slowest, most reliable       Layer 3: Interactive User Dialog (approve / reject / edit)

                          Figure 5: Claude Code’s three-layered permission system.

    For background and forked sub-agents, only layers 1–2 are available—their would-be prompts
resolve to denials—while default foreground sub-agents can still surface interactive dialogs. Unre-
solvable cases escalate to the parent coordinator. A denial tracking mechanism counts permission
refusals per session; after N denials, the system falls back to prompting. Each async agent maintains
local denial state to prevent cross-agent pollution.

10.2     Codex: A Four-Layer Permission Stack with Native Sandboxing
The April edition described Codex’s safety as two mechanisms—policy rules plus OS sandbox—
and characterized its approval gate as “near-invisible.” The July snapshot shows four layers, two of
them converging on Claude Code’s design:

Layer 1: Execution Policy (Starlark, not TOML). Executable rules (execpolicy/)
are written in Starlark: prefix_rule(pattern=[...], decision="allow|prompt|forbidden",
match=[...], not_match=[...]) and network_rule(...) functions, loaded from CODEX_HOME/rules/
and per-config-layer rules directories.7 A distinctive detail: rules may carry inline match/not_match
examples that are validated at parse time—executable test cases inside the policy file.
1  prefix_rule (
2      pattern = [" git " , " status "] ,
 3     decision = " allow " ,
 4     match = [[" git " , " status "] , [" git " , " status " , " - - short "]] ,
 5     not_match = [[" git " , " push "]] ,
 6 )
 7 network_rule (
 8     protocol = " https " ,
 9     host = "*. github . com " ,
10     decision = " allow " ,
11 )

                          Listing 2: Codex execution policy example (Starlark).

Layer 2: Lifecycle Hooks. A hooks crate exposes external hooks whose event vocabulary is
near-verbatim Claude Code’s: PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PostToolUse, PreCompact,
SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, Stop—plus a PostCompact
event with no Claude Code counterpart—with block/allow decision outputs. Section 14.5 dis-
cusses this as the corpus’s clearest case of one provider-native harness adopting another’s extension
interface as a de facto standard.

Layer 3: Guardian, an LLM Approval Reviewer. When a command would require user
approval, a dedicated Guardian session re-assesses the exact planned action against a policy prompt
(compact transcript reconstruction, strict-JSON verdict), fails closed on timeout or malformed
output, and carries a per-turn rejection circuit breaker. The “no LLM classifier” contrast the April
edition drew against Claude Code no longer holds: both provider-native flagships now implement
the static-rules → LLM-classifier → interactive/OS backstop pattern. A user-facing collaboration-
mode selector (Plan/Default presets that mask model, reasoning effort, and developer instructions)
completes the convergence: all four provider-native systems now ship a read-only planning mode.

Layer 4: Native OS Sandboxing.                 The sandbox implementation spans three platforms:

    • Linux: vendored, in-tree Bubblewrap (invoked via C FFI) with read-only filesystem
      (–ro-bind / /), writable roots via –bind, network namespace isolation (–unshare-net),
      user/PID namespace isolation; Landlock demoted to a legacy fallback.
    • macOS: Seatbelt profiles via /usr/bin/sandbox-exec with configurable allow/deny rules.
    • Windows: Restricted-token processes with ACL-based read/write restrictions.
    7
    The April edition rendered these rules as TOML; that was an error in our earlier audit—the policy language has
been Starlark throughout.

## Seite 37

Observation 6. OS-level sandboxing is one of the most code-expensive capabilities in the
corpus, and it is a choice rather than a consequence of scale. The April corpus suggested a
size correlation (its two largest systems were its two cross-platform sandboxers); the expanded
corpus breaks it. Hermes, among the largest systems here, ships zero OS-level isolation primi-
tives: it delegates containment to six pluggable execution backends and spends its safety budget
on content-borne threats instead (promptware scanning—pattern-matching for prompt-injection
payloads—a skills supply chain, a command-policy floor that survives –yolo). OpenCode,
comparably large, is policy-only, investing in syntax-aware command permissioning rather than
isolation. Pi documents the refusal as a security argument: a partial in-process sandbox “would
be easy to misunderstand as a security boundary.” What remains true is the cost side: where
native sandboxing is built (Codex, Gemini CLI; Claude Code wraps Anthropic’s reusable
sandbox-runtime as an opt-in), it is a substantial multi-thousand-line investment—and Sec-
tion 14.4 shows the meta-harness paying the same bill a second time, one layer up.

10.3   OpenHands: Ensemble Defense-in-Depth
OpenHands’s pluggable SecurityAnalyzer framework matured substantially in the V1 SDK.
The Invariant analyzer of the V0 era is gone; the current set pairs an LLMSecurityAnalyzer
(the agent self-rates each action’s security_risk, a parameter the system prompt instructs it
to fill) and a GraySwanAnalyzer (external adversarial API) with two new deterministic analyzers—
PatternSecurityAnalyzer and PolicyRailSecurityAnalyzer, the latter shipping named rails
such as fetch-to-exec, raw-disk-op, and catastrophic-delete over shell-AST parsing. An
EnsembleSecurityAnalyzer fuses verdicts worst-case-wins, with broken child analyzers failing
closed to HIGH. The LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH/UNKNOWN risk enum survives; confirmation is now
a policy object (AlwaysConfirm/NeverConfirm/ConfirmRisky). The prompt side completes a two-
sided injection defense: repository-derived context is wrapped in <UNTRUSTED_CONTENT> markers,
and a dedicated prompt section teaches the risk-assessment protocol.

10.4   OpenClaw: Scope-Based Authorization
OpenClaw implements scope-based authorization with operator and node connection roles
over namespaced scopes (operator.read/write/admin/pairing/. . . ). The gateway enforces per-
method scope requirements. Additional safety mechanisms include: fixed-window rate limiting per
IP/token, SSRF policy enforcement, DM allowlist with pairing approval workflow, exec approval
gates for browser actions and plugin actions, and chat sanitization. The 2MB MAX_PROMPT_BYTES
limit provides DoS protection (CWE-400).

10.5   Gemini CLI: Four Approval Modes Plus Cross-Platform Sandbox
Gemini CLI layers two complementary safety mechanisms. First, an ApprovalMode enum gates
every tool call into one of four modes:

  • PLAN: Read-only; the model sees the full tool list but can only invoke read tools (Glob,
    Read, Grep, etc.). Its response is presented as a plan, and the user must explicitly approve
    before exiting plan mode.
  • DEFAULT: Interactive approval dialog per tool call; users can approve once, approve always,
    or reject.
  • AUTO_EDIT: Edit operations are auto-approved while shell and other side-effecting tools
    still prompt; intended for fast iteration on local code.
  • YOLO: All actions auto-approved. Intended for CI/scripted use only.

Second, a SandboxPolicyManager enforces TOML-based per-mode policies: which paths are read-
able/writable, which network hosts are reachable, which environment variables are scrubbed. The

                                               37

## Seite 38

combination is structurally similar to Codex’s policy-as-code + sandbox stack but layers an ex-
plicit user-facing mode selector on top—an ergonomic that Codex itself has since adopted with
its collaboration-mode presets. A separate isTrustedFolder() check further widens or narrows
context-discovery scope based on whether the directory is in the user’s trust list, providing a fourth
layer of opt-in granularity. The release cadence between our snapshots was dominated by policy-
engine and supply-chain hardening—trust-gated .env loading in headless mode, shell-command
validation with a core-tools allowlist, skill-install path-traversal checks—supporting Observation 6’s
claim that safety absorbs a disproportionate share of engineering in the largest systems.

10.6    Mistral Vibe: Permission-Scope Patterns Plus Agent-Profile Gates
Mistral Vibe has no OS sandbox (an opt-in –worktree flag now provides branch-level isolation)
but compensates with a finer-grained permission model than the other no-sandbox systems. Each
tool call is checked against a hierarchy:
  1. Tool-wide permission setting (ALWAYS, ASK, NEVER) at the agent-profile level.
  2. Tool-specific validators (e.g., resolve_file_tool_permission pattern-matches paths), plus
     a default read-only command allowlist that auto-approves ls/cat/grep-class commands.
  3. User-declared shell hooks (hooks.toml, before_tool) that can deny a call or rewrite its
     inputs before permission evaluation.
  4. Session rules added at runtime—now persisted across sessions for “always allow” grants.
  5. An interactive approval callback presented to the user unless bypass_tool_permissions (the
     renamed auto_approve) is set.
Agent profiles bake in safety classifications: plan and chat profiles are SAFE (read-only); default is
NEUTRAL; accept-edits is DESTRUCTIVE; auto-approve is YOLO. Tools can also override the agent
default: write_file forces ASK for sensitive patterns (.env files) regardless of profile. There is no
LLM-based risk classifier and no OS-level isolation; safety reduces to explicit per-pattern matching,
hooks, and user prompts.

10.7    Hermes: A Policy Floor That Survives YOLO
Hermes inverts the sandbox question: the largest Python system in the corpus ships zero OS-
level isolation primitives—no Seatbelt, Landlock, seccomp, or Bubblewrap anywhere in its tools
tree—delegating isolation to its six pluggable execution backends. On the local backend, safety
is policy-as-code at scale: a 3,200-line approval module whose documentation states “config.yaml
IS the security policy.” Its layers: user deny-globs; a twelve-pattern hardline floor (rm -rf
/, mkfs, dd to block devices, fork bombs, shutdown) that survives –yolo—the YOLO environ-
ment variable is frozen at module import precisely so a prompt-injected skill cannot flip it at
runtime; 47 dangerous-command patterns matched on deobfuscated variants (quote-splice removal,
command-substitution folding, command-position anchoring); an external Rust content scanner
(Tirith, cosign-verified install); and an optional auxiliary-LLM gate (_smart_approve: temper-
ature 0, 16 max tokens, APPROVE/DENY/ESCALATE—its code credits Codex’s Smart Ap-
provals). The distinctive threat model is content-borne: promptware scanning of context files,
memory writes, MCP tool descriptions, and skill installs (with builtin/trusted/community trust
tiers and quarantine); SSRF guards that always block cloud metadata endpoints; untrusted tool
results wrapped in <untrusted_tool_result> delimiters with lookalike defanging. Container back-
ends skip the dangerous-command layer entirely—until a host bind-mount re-enters it. Notable
absences: no per-tool allow/ask/deny matrix, no append-only audit log.

10.8    Pi: Documented Absence as a Security Argument
Pi is the corpus’s only system that documents the absence of safety infrastructure as a design
principle: its security documentation argues that a partial in-process sandbox “would be easy to

                                                 38

---

## Seite 39

misunderstand as a security boundary,” declares prompt injection via context files unprotectable,
and lets built-in tools execute unconditionally with the invoking user’s permissions. The one built-
in gate is project trust: repo-controlled configuration (extensions, skills, prompts, themes) loads
only from trusted paths, decided per canonical path with nearest-ancestor lookup—explicitly “not
a sandbox,” and context files load regardless. Permissioning is policy-as-code taken literally: the
tool_call extension event exposes mutable tool arguments and a {block, reason} veto, and the
reference permission-gate example implements the familiar regex-plus-confirm flow (rm -rf, sudo,
chmod 777) in ∼80 lines of user space; isolation, when wanted, arrives as extensions (Anthropic’s
sandbox-runtime, a QEMU micro-VM) through the per-tool Operations seam. The append-only
session tree doubles as a complete audit trail.

10.9    OpenCode: Syntax-Aware Permissioning, Permissive by Default
OpenCode is, after Hermes, the second-largest system shipping no OS-level isolation (“sandbox”
in its code means git worktrees), and its default posture is the inverse of Codex’s: "*": allow
inside the project, with asks reserved for external_directory access, .env reads, and doom loops.
Its distinctive investment is syntax-aware command permissioning: every bash command is parsed
with web-tree-sitter (bash and PowerShell grammars); the exact command text becomes the ask pat-
tern, while “always allow” grants are scoped by a ∼130-entry, explicitly LLM-generated command-
arity dictionary (git→2, npm run→3), producing grants like git commit * rather than blanket
approval; file-manipulating commands get their argument paths resolved, and out-of-project paths
raise external_directory asks. Permission rules ({permission, pattern, action}, last-match-
wins over glob wildcards) are layered defaults → built-in agent → user config → per-agent → per-
session, and denying "*" for a tool removes it from the LLM’s view entirely—tool availability itself
is permission-derived. A parallel v2 engine inverts to deny-by-default and persists approvals to
SQLite; headless runs auto-reject all asks. There is no dangerous-command denylist and no risk
classifier.

10.10    Minimal Safety (Aider, Mini-SWE-Agent)
Aider offers an interactive confirmation mode but no automated risk assessment. However, its
reflection loop with three-stage Python linting (syntax → compile → flake8) provides implicit safety
by catching errors before they propagate.
    Mini-SWE-Agent implements only resource limits as safety mechanisms—step_limit,
cost_limit, and (added in the v2.4 line) a wall-clock limit and a consecutive-format-error cap,
plus an opt-in interactive confirm mode—sufficient for benchmark evaluation but inadequate for
production use.

11      Multi-Agent Orchestration
Nine of the eleven systems support multi-agent execution, and their architectures diverge substan-
tially. This is the dimension on which the corpus is most spread out, so we go into more detail here
than in the other sections.

11.1    Multi-Agent Taxonomy
We identify six distinct multi-agent patterns:

  1. Single-agent (no multi-agent): Mini-SWE-Agent, Aider—and Pi’s core, which ships
     no spawn or task tool; its sub-agents live in extension space (below).
  2. Sequential delegation: Mistral Vibe (parent spawns a sub-agent via the task tool and
     awaits completion).

                                                 39

## Seite 40

   3. Parallel child sessions: OpenHands (task and delegate tools run children as separate
      conversations, concurrently in threads), OpenCode (task creates child sessions running the
      same loop; multiple calls in one message execute concurrently).
   4. Hierarchical thread tree with fan-out: Codex (dedicated threads, fork-mode-controlled
      inheritance, per-model tool generations, map-reduce fan-out, persisted parent/child topology).
   5. Recursive composition: Claude Code (agents spawn sub-agents composably, with
      prompt-cache-sharing forks).
   6. Registry + cross-process protocol: Gemini CLI (named agent definitions behind a sym-
      metric local/remote session protocol, remote agents via A2A), OpenClaw (ACP session
      spawn), Hermes’s Kanban swarm (subprocesses over a SQLite blackboard).

11.2       Deep Dive: Claude Code Recursive Composition
Claude Code’s multi-agent architecture is the most sophisticated among the systems studied. It
supports three levels of coordination: ad-hoc sub-agents, typed agent definitions, and full coordina-
tor mode.

11.2.1       Agent Definitions System
Agents are defined via a JSON/Zod schema specifying a description, prompt, optional tool
whitelist/blacklist, model selection, turn limits, permission mode, MCP server bindings, isolation
level, background execution flag, and skills.
    Agent definitions are loaded from a priority hierarchy: built-in agents → plugin agents →
user settings → project settings → flag settings → policy/managed agents. Later sources override
earlier ones. Built-in agents include Explore (fast codebase search), Plan (architecture design), and
VerificationAgent (test execution).

11.2.2       Context Forking
When a sub-agent is spawned via AgentTool, the parent’s context is forked along six dimensions:

  1. AbortController: New controller linked to parent (parent abort → child abort, but not vice
     versa).
  2. File State Cache: LRU cache cloned to prevent concurrent mutation.
  3. Permission Prompts: Suppressed for async agents (shouldAvoidPermissionPrompts =
     true).
  4. App State: Set to no-op for async agents to prevent dead session mutation.
  5. Denial Tracking: Fresh local state (refusals don’t accumulate globally).

                                                                 41

---

## Seite 42

  6. Tool Decisions: Fresh Map per agent (no cross-agent pollution).

    A critical optimization is prompt cache sharing: the parent’s renderedSystemPrompt is
frozen at fork time and passed verbatim to the child. This ensures prompt cache hits are maintained
across fork/resume boundaries, preventing GrowthBook feature gate divergence from invalidating
caches.

11.2.3    Coordinator Mode
When activated (via environment variable or feature gate), a Lead agent orchestrates Workers

    Workers are restricted to a 16-tool whitelist (ASYNC_AGENT_ALLOWED_TOOLS): FileRead, Web-
Search, TodoWrite, Grep, WebFetch, Glob, the two shell tools (Bash and PowerShell), FileEdit,
FileWrite, NotebookEdit, Skill, SyntheticOutput, ToolSearch, EnterWorktree, and ExitWorktree.
The coordinator synthesizes worker findings before delegating the next phase, following a structured
workflow: Research → Synthesis → Implementation → Verification.

11.3     Deep Dive: Codex Thread Tree Model
Codex’s multi-agent architecture is built around three core abstractions:

AgentControl      is the central control plane for spawning and managing sub-agents.

AgentRegistry       tracks all live agents in a session tree, maintaining LiveAgent metadata structs.

Spawn Flow. The spawn_agent_internal() function reserves a spawn slot, inherits the parent’s
sandbox and execution policy, resolves fork mode and metadata from the source, creates a thread
with the appropriate history (full, truncated, or fresh), and emits a session-started notification.

SpawnAgentForkMode. A distinctive feature is SpawnAgentForkMode, which controls how
much conversation history is inherited by sub-agents:

  • FullHistory: Inherit all messages (full context).
  • LastNTurns(N): Inherit only the most recent N turns (reduced context).

   Message filtering (keep_forked_rollout_item()) preserves only system/developer/user mes-
sages and final assistant answers, filtering out intermediate tool calls and reasoning. This selective
inheritance prevents context bloat in sub-agents.

                                                            42

## Seite 43

Inter-Agent Communication. The dedicated mailbox module of early versions has been folded
into the session’s input queue: inter-agent messages flow through InputQueue activities with mailbox
delivery phases, carried as typed InterAgentCommunication records (Spawn/Message/Followup/Result).
Two tool generations coexist—multi_agents (spawn/wait/send_message/interrupt/list) and
multi_agents_v2 (spawn/wait/send_input/resume_agent/close_agent)—selected per model via
a multi_agent_version field in the model metadata, and parent/child topology is persisted by a
dedicated agent-graph-store crate. The parent monitors child status via an AgentStatus enum.

Fan-Out and Declarative Roles. Beyond spawn and mailbox, Codex has grown map-reduce-
style orchestration: spawn_agents_on_csv launches one sub-agent per CSV row under a shared
JSON-schema result contract with concurrency normalization and runtime caps, folding results
back via report_agent_job_result. Sub-agents are typed by declarative TOML roles (built-in
explorer and worker roles ship active in-tree; an awaiter role file remains but is currently un-
registered) applied as high-precedence configuration layers—Codex’s answer to Claude Code’s
agent definitions—and delegation itself is model-governed: the ultra reasoning tier couples max-
imum reasoning with automatic task delegation, and configurable delegation modes (disabled /
explicit-request-only / proactive) apply at thread and turn level.

11.4   OpenHands: Parallel Delegation over Conversation Trees
The V0-era AgentDelegateAction (sequential, one delegate at a time, shared event stream) is gone.
The V1 SDK delegates through tools: a TaskTool whose shape is conspicuously Claude Code-like
(prompt, subagent_type, description, resume), with a TaskManager creating a separate conver-
sation per task (own event log, metrics synced back), and a DelegateTool with spawn/delegate
commands that runs delegated tasks concurrently in threads. Sub-agents are declared as Markdown
files with YAML frontmatter (name, description, model, tools, skills, hooks, MCP config, per-
mission mode, condenser) at project/user/builtin/plugin levels—built-ins include code-explorer,
bash-runner, and web-researcher (plus a general-purpose default)—and nesting is explicitly
supported. Above the delegation layer sits a scaffold-level outer loop: a /goal endpoint runs an
LLM judge over the transcript after each run, either injecting a follow-up prompt or stopping with
a completion status, complemented by pluggable critics with configurable refinement-iteration caps.

11.5   Mistral Vibe Sequential Subagent Delegation
Mistral Vibe’s multi-agent support is intentionally simple: a parent agent invokes the task
tool, which constructs a fresh AgentLoop instance with the requested agent profile (e.g., explore),
runs it to completion in-process, and returns the sub-agent’s AssistantEvent outputs and
ToolResultEvent summaries to the parent. A guard enforces that only profiles tagged as “sub-
agent” (currently just explore) can be delegated to, preventing accidental recursive escalation to
write-capable profiles. Each sub-agent gets a fresh VibeConfig, its own session directory, and an
independent message history, providing isolation comparable to Codex’s thread tree but at the
cost of true parallelism: the parent blocks on await until the sub-agent exits. The architectural
simplicity (one tool, sequential, in-process) means Mistral Vibe sits on the simplicity end of the
multi-agent spectrum—the corpus’s simplest delegation short of none, reminiscent of OpenHands’s
retired V0 AgentDelegateAction.

11.6   Gemini CLI: Registry, Symmetric Session Protocol, and A2A
Gemini CLI’s multi-agent model splits across two layers. Locally, an AgentRegistry holds named
agent definitions—Markdown files with mandatory YAML frontmatter—loaded from user, project,
and extension scopes. The built-in generalist agent, for example, grants access to all registered
tools with a 10-minute, 20-turn run budget. Invocation flows through the /agent slash command,
@agent-name prompt notation, or—since the sub-agent unification of v0.39—a model-invocable
invoke_agent tool, each run receiving an isolated tool registry. The invocation path has been

                                                43

---

## Seite 44

abstracted behind an agent session protocol with symmetric local and remote implementations, so
a registry entry backed by an in-process executor and one backed by a remote A2A agent are driven
through the same interface.
    Where Gemini CLI diverges from every other system in our corpus is the packages/a2a-server
module, an experimental implementation of Google’s Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol. A2A is to
inter-agent communication what MCP is to tool integration: a JSON-RPC standard for one agent
process to discover, authenticate to, and exchange messages with another, possibly on a different
machine and built by a different vendor. Gemini CLI’s A2A server lets a remote orchestrator drive a
local Gemini CLI instance as if it were a registered local agent—now with usage metadata reported
over the protocol for cross-vendor resource accounting—opening the door to cross-vendor multi-
agent topologies that no other corpus system supports natively (the meta-harness of Section 14.4
builds exactly such topologies from outside).

11.7    Hermes: Guarded Delegation, Swarms, and Mixture-of-Agents
Hermes is flat-by-default delegation with two escape hatches upward. delegate_task builds
child agents in-process on a thread pool: fresh conversation, focused system prompt, summary-
only return, toolsets intersected with the parent’s (“subagent must not gain tools the parent
lacks”), and a six-tool blocklist (no recursion, no user interaction, no memory writes, no schedul-
ing). Defaults are conservative—three concurrent children, 50-iteration budgets, depth 1—but a
role="orchestrator" configuration plus a spawn-depth setting unlocks nested trees, with the or-
chestrator prompt block explicitly “modeled on OpenClaw’s buildSubagentSystemPrompt.” Back-
ground delegation returns a handle and re-enters as a fresh turn through a completion queue rather
than splicing mid-turn—a prompt-cache-preserving choice. Above this sits a process-level tier: the
Kanban swarm runs planning-root → parallel workers → verifier → synthesizer as separate hermes
-p <profile> subprocesses coordinated through a SQLite board and a blackboard of structured
JSON comments—coordinator-worker via shared database rather than protocol or channel. A third
overlay, /moa, fans out advisory reference models (up to eight concurrently) whose outputs season
the main model’s next iteration.

11.8    Pi: Sub-Agents as an Extension, Fleets as a Package
Core Pi has no spawn or task tool—sub-agents are the flagship demonstration of its extension
thesis, shipped as a ∼1,000-line example. Each invocation spawns a separate pi –mode json -p
–no-session OS process, giving hard context isolation by construction; the parent parses the
child’s JSONL stdout for progress and cost aggregation. One tool offers three shapes: single,
parallel (worker pool of four, max eight tasks), and chain with {previous} substitution. Agent
definitions are Markdown-plus-frontmatter with tool filtering via the child’s –tools flag; there is no
depth counter and no mid-run parent-child messaging. Above the single process, an experimental
orchestrator package supervises fleets of Pi instances in RPC mode and registers presence with
a hosted coordinator—multi-instance management rather than an in-loop coordinator. Notably,
when Pi does do multi-agent, it lands on cross-process JSONL rather than in-process primitives—a
data point Section 13.3 returns to.

11.9    OpenCode: Child Sessions with Permission-Derived Capabilities
OpenCode’s sub-agents are child sessions, not a separate engine: the task tool creates a Ses-
sion with a parentID running the same loop, resumable via task_id, returning only the final
assistant text wrapped in <task_result> XML; background results are injected as synthetic
user messages. Agents and modes are unified in one schema (mode: primary|subagent|all):
built-ins are build, plan (edit denied except plan files), general, read-only explore, plus
hidden compaction/title/summary utility agents—plan mode is a permission ruleset plus a
<system-reminder> injection, not an architectural overlay. Tool availability is everywhere
permission-derived (denying "*" for a tool removes it from the LLM’s view), and containment

                                                 44

---

## Seite 45

is asymmetric: children inherit only the parent’s deny rules. Recursion is off by default (task
auto-denied to children) but opt-in per agent with no numeric depth cap; custom agents come
from config, Markdown files, or—uniquely—LLM generation (generateObject over {identifier,
whenToUse, systemPrompt}).

11.10    OpenClaw Session-Based Orchestration
OpenClaw’s multi-agent model is fundamentally different: it operates through an ACP (Agent
Client Protocol, Zed/Google’s editor-oriented JSON-RPC standard at agentclientprotocol.com, not
IBM’s older homonymous Agent Communication Protocol) translator that bridges the Gateway wire
protocol to agent processes. Sub-agents are spawned as child processes with RPC binding. Each
agent gets its own session with JSONL transcript persistence. Communication occurs via ACP delta
events (text, thought, tool calls) rather than shared memory. A rate limiter (MAX_PROMPT_BYTES =
2MB) provides DoS protection.
Observation 7. Coordinator-worker emerges independently across the corpus: in all four
provider-native systems (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Mistral Vibe), in Open-
Hands (parallel delegation over conversation trees), in Hermes (configuration-gated orchestra-
tor role plus a subprocess swarm over a SQLite blackboard—a novel coordination substrate),
in OpenCode (concurrent child sessions), and in OpenClaw at the protocol layer. We use
coordinator-worker broadly here, for any parent-spawns-workers delegation; Section 6’s narrower
prescriptive overlay applies to Claude Code, Codex, and (gated) Hermes only. So many
independently developed codebases converging on the same hierarchical shape is strong evidence
of convergent evolution—though the convergence should be scoped to systems that build multi-
agent into core: Pi is a production SWE harness that deliberately ships single-agent, relegating
sub-agents to extension space. The implementations diverge instructively in what they optimize:
Claude Code forks context and shares the prompt cache across children (cost); Codex builds
a depth-tracked thread tree with typed inter-agent records, per-model tool generations, and CSV
fan-out (isolation and scale); Gemini CLI abstracts invocation behind a symmetric local/remote
session protocol (portability); Mistral Vibe runs sub-agents in-process and sequentially (sim-
plicity); Hermes intersects toolsets and blocklists recursion by default (containment). Hadfield
et al. [17] describe orchestrator-worker as the natural pattern for “valuable tasks that involve
heavy parallelization, information that exceeds single context windows, and interfacing with
numerous complex tools,” which is a fair description of a long-horizon coding session.

11.11    Orchestration Pipelines: Claude Code vs. Codex
Claude Code and Codex are the two dominant commercial coding agents, each representing
the state of the art in its provider’s ecosystem. Their orchestration pipelines, end-to-end from
user request to completed task, take very different design positions. Table 18 highlights the key
divergences.
    The table reveals two coherent philosophies whose gap narrowed measurably between our snap-
shots. Claude Code is compositional-prescriptive: it enforces structured phases (Research → Syn-
thesis → Implementation → Verification), restricts sub-agent capabilities via tool whitelists, com-
poses agents recursively, and optimizes aggressively around prompt-cache economics. Codex was
sandboxed-emergent—safety guaranteed at the OS level, workflow organization left to the model—
but has grown prescriptive structure of its own: a user-facing collaboration-mode selector with a
Plan preset, declarative sub-agent roles, depth-tracked spawn control, and a Guardian classifier that
mirrors Claude Code’s middle permission layer, while Claude Code’s hook vocabulary and plu-
gin format have become Codex interfaces (Section 14.5). Both produce strong results on real-world
benchmarks; the residual philosophical difference is where safety is guaranteed (OS enforcement vs.
layered review), not how workflows are organized.

## Seite 46

12     Extensibility Mechanisms
Every system in the corpus provides extension points, though through quite different mechanisms.

12.1    Plugin Architectures
OpenClaw provides the most mature plugin architecture in the corpus—and since the spring 2026
releases, an externalized one: official provider and channel plugins were cut over to standalone first-
class npm packages with manifest-first metadata, moving model catalogs and routing tables out of
core. Plugins are manifest-driven (openclaw.plugin.json), discovered in the workspace directory,
loaded dynamically via jiti, and registered through typed SDK contracts:

  • Channel plugins: Implement ChannelEntry (receive, send, status, configure).
  • Provider plugins: Implement ProviderEntry (inference stream).
  • Skill plugins: Register via capability system.

    Strict import boundaries are enforced: extension production code may only import the public
plugin-SDK surface and local API barrels. Direct imports of src/** are prohibited.
    OpenClaw is, however, no longer alone in the manifest-driven-plugin camp. Codex’s plugin
architecture expanded substantially between our snapshots: a marketplace-add pipeline (GitHub,
git, local paths, URLs), a model-callable in-conversation approval tool (request_plugin_install),
.claude-plugin format compatibility, and workspace-level sharing joined an already-present plugin
manager; plugins contribute tools, skills, and lifecycle hooks. OpenHands’s plugin system makes
the convergence explicit: its plugins bundle skills, hooks, MCP config, agents, and commands, and
its manifest loader accepts the directories [".plugin", ".claude-plugin"] with plugin.json—it
deliberately reads Claude Code’s plugin format, the clearest interoperability-by-adoption case in
the corpus. Claude Code itself supports MCP servers (for external tools), skills (for specialized
workflows), and agent definitions (for custom agent types) via a JSON/Zod schema with built-in,
custom, and plugin sources (Section 11.2). Pi relocates the entire question: extensions are runtime-
loaded TypeScript modules against an API of ∼33 typed events spanning session lifecycle, tool inter-
ception (blocking and in-place argument mutation), whole-context rewriting, and—unusually—raw
provider I/O surgery (before_provider_request, after_provider_response); the repo ships 78
examples that are, feature for feature, other harnesses’ built-ins, most at 1–16 KB each, distributed
through a package manager (pi install npm:...|git:...). OpenCode’s plugins are async func-
tions returning ∼20 typed hooks (chat.params, tool.execute.before/after, tool.definition
rewriting, multi-step OAuth auth flows), executed sequentially for determinism; custom tools need
no plugin at all—any .opencode/tool/*.ts export becomes a tool.

Gemini CLI: Extensions + Slash Commands + Early MCP Adoption. Gemini CLI
ships an explicit ExtensionLoader interface backed by the GeminiCLIExtension type. Extensions
can contribute custom tools (typically via MCP), slash commands, hooks, skills, and GEMINI.md
snippets, and are discovered from the ~/.gemini/extensions/ directory. Gemini CLI was an early
adopter of MCP, with first-class implementations for stdio-spawned local servers, SSE connections,
and Streamable HTTP transports, plus built-in auth providers (google-credentials, OAuth).
MCP support extends beyond tools to prompts and resources (the broader MCP spec), which
most other systems’ adapters omit. Slash commands (/agent, /mcp, /skill, /memory, /help) are
themselves extensible via skill metadata, allowing extensions to register new commands.

Mistral Vibe: Skills, MCP, Custom Tools, Agents, and Hooks. Mistral Vibe’s
extensibility surface has grown to five orthogonal axes. Skills follow the agentskills.io spec-
ification [43]: each is a directory containing a SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter, discovered
from .agents/skills/, .vibe/skills/, ~/.vibe/skills/, ~/.agents/skills/, and any user-
configured paths—now supplemented by built-in skills (including a “self-awareness” skill that

                                                  46

---

## Seite 47

documents the harness to itself) and a remote registry client that installs versioned skills from
a hosted catalog. See Section 12.5 for full cross-system comparison. MCP servers are declared
as [[mcp_servers]] blocks supporting http, streamable-http, and stdio transports, with
tools namespaced as {server_name}_{tool_name} and permissioned identically to built-ins; the
layer matured between snapshots into a managed integration surface—OAuth login flows driven
from the TUI (/mcp add|login|logout|status), a curated registry of hosted Mistral “connec-
tors,” and an MCP sampling handler that lets connected servers borrow Mistral Vibe’s LLM
backend for their own completions, a reverse dependency no other corpus system implements.
Custom tools can be added via path-based discovery (tool_paths); custom system prompts as
~/.vibe/prompts/{prompt_id}.md; and custom agents as ~/.vibe/agents/{agent_name}.toml
with a deep-merge override mechanism on the base config—itself now part of an explicit
configuration-layer stack (default, user TOML, trusted-project .vibe/config.toml, VIBE_*
environment, runtime overrides, agent profile). The fifth axis is user-facing lifecycle hooks:
before_tool/after_tool/post_agent_turn shell hooks declared in hooks.toml can deny a
tool call, rewrite its inputs, or append context—a direct structural sibling of Claude Code’s
PreToolUse/PostToolUse, layered on top of (not replacing) the internal middleware pipeline.

12.2   Protocol-Based Interfaces
Mini-SWE-Agent uses Python Protocols for structural subtyping: any class implementing the
Model, Agent, or Environment protocol can be substituted without inheritance. This is the lightest-
weight extensibility mechanism, requiring no registration, no manifest, and no SDK, just interface
conformance.

12.3   Configuration-Driven Extensibility
Aider’s model registry contains per-model metadata for 350+ models, including edit format, weak
model name, cache control settings, extra API parameters, reasoning tag handling, and editor model
configuration. This data-driven approach enables support for new models without code changes.
    Codex’s layered TOML configuration now extends above the user: mobile-device-management
(MDM), host-wide system, and enterprise cloud-delivered layers enter as base defaults beneath user
(config.toml plus named profiles), project (.codex directory), and session-flag scopes, while a
separately composed requirements/constraint engine (fed from the same MDM, system, and cloud
sources) validates and can hard-restrict what the lower layers may set. It is the most enterprise-
governance-oriented configuration model in the corpus. Mistral Vibe now mirrors the layered
approach (six layers merged by a ConfigBuilder with per-field merge strategies), making explicit
config-layer stacks a two-system pattern.
    OpenClaw’s config system is the most complex in the corpus: a Zod-validated openclaw.json
with hundreds of nested structures, plus a large auto-generated TypeScript file of validation rules
for all bundled channels alongside a hand-maintained schema-help surface.

12.4   Model Context Protocol (MCP)
MCP remains a cross-cutting extension mechanism, supported by Claude Code, Codex, Gem-
ini CLI, Mistral Vibe, OpenHands, Hermes, OpenCode, and OpenClaw—8 of 11 systems (7
of 10 coding-first). OpenHands implements MCP via MCPToolAction/MCPToolObservation event
types, with a single MCPServer model validating four transports (stdio, http, streamable-http,
sse) and first-class authentication up to full OAuth flows with token state. Hermes’s support
is near-complete (stdio/Streamable HTTP/SSE, resources, prompts, sampling, elicitation, OAuth;
only prompt-list-change notifications ignored), and Hermes is itself an MCP server, matching
OpenClaw’s channel bridge. OpenCode covers tools, prompts, resources, and resource templates
with OAuth dynamic client registration (sampling and elicitation explicitly disabled with tracking-
issue comments). The corpus’s one principled holdout is Pi, whose documentation rejects MCP

                                                47

## Seite 48

outright—“build CLI tools with READMEs”—making skills-plus-shell its articulated alternative to
a wire protocol.

12.5   Skills as an Emerging Capability-Bundle Standard
Alongside MCP, a second cross-cutting extensibility mechanism has shown up in the corpus: skills.
MCP standardizes how an agent talks to an external tool process; skills standardize how an agent
packages a unit of expertise into a discoverable directory (instructions, optional scripts, optional
tool whitelists, metadata) that can be dropped into a project or user home and picked up by the
agent at discovery time. Mitra et al. [80] frame the same idea from the training side: skills as
teachable units in agentic flows. Nine of the eleven systems implement some form of skills system;
only Aider and Mini-SWE-Agent omit it (Table 10).

Convergence on the SKILL.md format and the .agents/skills/ path. The format is
essentially universal among the nine adopters: a directory named after the skill, containing a

## Seite 50

the canonical agentskills.io location, is accepted by six systems (Mistral Vibe, Gemini CLI,
OpenClaw, OpenHands, Pi, OpenCode), and the vendor-specific homes (~/.claude/skills/,
~/.gemini/skills/, ~/.vibe/skills/, ~/.hermes/skills/, ~/.pi/agent/skills/, ~/.openclaw/skills/)
coexist with project-local equivalents. The sharpest interoperability datum: OpenCode deliber-
ately searches a competitor’s home—its discovery list includes ~/.claude/skills and .claude/
directories, so skills installed for Claude Code work in OpenCode unmodified.

Skills versus MCP: the tie has broken. MCP and skills address different layers. MCP is
a wire protocol for an agent to talk to a separately running process that exposes tools, prompts,
and resources; skills are a file-system convention for packaging an instruction-plus-script bundle the
agent reads directly. The two compose: Claude Code’s skill registry deduplicates MCP-supplied
prompts that look like skills, and Mistral Vibe composes in the other direction, letting MCP
servers borrow its LLM via sampling while skills arrive from a hosted registry. In April the two
standards were tied at 6/8 adoption; the expanded July corpus breaks the tie in skills’ favor—skills
9/11, MCP 8/11—because Pi implements agentskills.io while rejecting MCP outright. Skills-as-
MCP-replacement is now an articulated position, not a coexistence.

Deferred loading as the dominant pattern. Echoing Claude Code’s deferred tool load-
ing (Section 8.3), eight of the nine adopters now load only skill metadata eagerly and fetch
bodies on demand—via a dedicated tool (SkillTool, ActivateSkill, skill, OpenHands’s
invoke_skill), via $-mention and implicit-invocation detection (Codex), via a three-tier dis-
closure chain (Hermes), or, most minimally, via the ordinary read tool against an XML index
(Pi). OpenHands, an eager outlier in April, moved to progressive disclosure with the V1 SDK;
OpenClaw remains the one eager loader, compensating with eligibility gating so ineligible skills
never reach the prompt.

Gating and conditional activation. The most architecturally interesting variation is condi-
tional activation. OpenClaw’s skills declare runtime requirements (binaries on PATH, environment
variables, OS family) and are filtered at load time, preventing “how to use kubectl” from pol-
luting the prompt on a machine without it. Claude Code’s paths frontmatter activates a skill
when the model touches matching files (via the Read, Edit, or Write tools), and OpenHands now
implements the same idea as PathTrigger rules injected on file-touch—marrying skills to the JIT
context philosophy of [19]. This is a structural advance over MCP, which treats every connected
server symmetrically regardless of whether its tools are relevant to the current task.

Skills grow a supply chain—and authors. Distribution has professionalized in one quarter.
Remote registries now exist in four systems (Mistral Vibe’s hosted catalog client, OpenCode’s
URL registries with versioned index caches, Hermes’s Skills Hub, OpenHands’s marketplace API),
and with distribution comes supply-chain security: Hermes applies trust tiers, pre-install static
scanning, quarantine, and dependency checks; OpenClaw routes installs through an approval work-
flow with provenance-verified sources; Gemini CLI hardened skill installs against path traversal;
Codex auto-installs a skill’s declared MCP-server dependencies (optionally after prompting). More
striking still, skills have acquired non-human authors: Hermes’s background-review agent creates
and patches skills from completed tasks (with a curator maintaining the collection), and Gem-
ini CLI’s extraction sub-agent mines sessions into skill patches for inbox review. The capability-
package layer is acquiring package-manager economics—registries, provenance, and now generated
packages—at remarkable speed.

Observation 8. Skills have overtaken MCP as the corpus’s most-adopted extensibility stan-
dard: 9/11 systems implement SKILL.md bundles (only Aider and Mini-SWE-Agent ab-
stain) versus 8/11 for MCP, the tie of April broken by Pi’s explicit skills-yes-MCP-no position.
Three second-order developments mark the layer’s maturation: deferred loading is now the near-
universal strategy (8 of 9 adopters); conditional activation (Claude Code paths, OpenHands
PathTrigger, OpenClaw requires) pushes JIT context engineering into the extensibility layer;
and a supply chain has emerged—hosted registries in four systems, trust tiers and quarantine
in Hermes, provenance verification in OpenClaw—together with the first agent-authored skills
(Hermes’s self-improving loop, Gemini CLI’s extraction inbox).

13     Cross-Cutting Observations and Implications
13.1   Architectural Pattern Catalog

13.2      The Twin Absences: No Agentic Frameworks, No Code RAG
Two technologies that the broader LLM-application literature treats as central to any production
agent turn out to be missing from all eleven systems.8 For this analysis, the absences are at least
as informative as the presences.

Absence 1: agentic frameworks. Every dependency manifest was inspected, and every source
tree grepped for imports of the widely deployed agentic frameworks: LangChain, LangGraph, Lla-
maIndex, AutoGen, CrewAI, Pydantic AI, Genkit, Haystack agents, Semantic Kernel, Google’s
ADK, and several smaller libraries (Smolagents, Swarm, Agno). Across roughly 4 M lines of Python,
TypeScript, and Rust, no production agent code path imports any of them—a result worth savor-
ing in two directions: Gemini CLI uses neither of Google’s own frameworks (Genkit, ADK), and
Hermes’s only “LangChain” strings sit inside bundled skill documentation teaching the agent how
users might use vector databases. Two boundary cases deserve precision. Aider ships one op-
tional framework-adjacent extra: its /help command can install llama-index to run doc-RAG
over aider’s own documentation—an opt-in feature dependency, not agent-loop orchestration. And
OpenCode delegates its inner LLM/tool plumbing to Vercel’s AI SDK—a provider-abstraction
layer, not an agent-orchestration framework, but the first corpus system whose inner loop plumb-
ing is a third-party SDK at all (an in-house replacement client sits behind a flag, suggesting the
dependency is transitional).
   8
    We expected to find at least some use of LangChain or another framework in the open-source projects. The uni-
formity surprised us; the search for counterexamples (vendored dependencies, dynamic imports, transpiled TypeScript
builds) ran for several weeks before we accepted the result. The July re-audit repeated the manifest and import sweep
across all twelve trees, including the three systems new to the corpus and the meta-harness.
